Reconfiguration of Brain Network Architectures between Resting-State and Complexity-Dependent Cognitive Reasoning.
Luke J. Hearne, Luca Cocchi, Andrew Zalesky, and Jason B. Mattingley.
The Journal of Neuroscience, August 30, 2017; 37(35):8399–8411.
DOI:10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0485-17.2017.

Our capacity for higher cognitive reasoning has a measurable limit. This limit is thought to arise from the brain’s capacity to flexibly reconfigure interactions between spatially distributed networks.
We found that increased reasoning demands rely on selective patterns of connectivity within cortical networks that emerged in addition to a more general, task-induced modular architecture.

Human participants (21 males and 28 females) underwent an initial resting-state scan, followed by a cognitive reasoning task involving different levels of complexity, followed by a second resting-state scan.

Sixty-five healthy, right-handed participants undertook the current study, of whom 49 were included in the final analysis (mean, 23.35 years; SD, 3.6 years; range, 18–33 years; 28 females).
Participants provided informed written consent to participate in the study. The research was approved by The University of Queensland Human Research Ethics Committee.

In the imaging session, participants underwent a resting-state scan, followed by three 12 min runs of the Latin Square Task (LST), a structural scan, and finally a second resting-state scan.
Participants also completed the Raven’s Advanced Progressive Matrices (40 min time limit), a standard and widely used measure of fluid intelligence.

The Latin Square Task (LST) is a nonverbal relational reasoning paradigm in which reasoning complexity is parametrically varied with minimal working-memory demands.
Each LST “puzzle” involves the presentation of a four-by-four matrix populated with a small number of geometric shapes (squares, circles, triangles, or crosses), blank spaces, and a single target, denoted by a yellow question mark.
Participants were asked to solve for the target according to the following rule: each shape can only occur once in every row and once in every column.
Null trials involved presentation of an LST grid, but instead of a target question mark, an asterisk was presented to cue the participant that no reasoning was required in this puzzle.
In total, 144 LST items were presented in the MR session across 16 blocks, with 36 items in each relational complexity condition (Null, Binary, Ternary, and Quaternary).
Administration of all items was pseudorandomized such that no two items of the same complexity occurred sequentially, and each block had two problems from each level of complexity.

Each trial contained a jittered fixation period, followed by an LST item, a second jittered fixation period, a response screen, and a confidence rating scale.
Fixation was presented for 4000 ms ± 586 ms, LST items were presented for 5000 ms, and the response and confidence screens were each presented for 2000 ms.

At the Centre for Advanced Imaging, The University of Queensland, imaging data were collected using a 7 T Siemens MR scanner fitted with a 32-channel head coil.
For both resting-state and task fMRI, whole-brain echo-planar images were acquired using a multiband sequence (acceleration factor, 5).
In each of the two resting scans, 1050 volumes were collected (~10 min each).
In each of the three runs of the task, 1250 volumes were collected (~12 min each) with the following parameters: voxel size, 2 mm3; TR = 586 ms; TE = 23 ms; flip angle, 40°; FOV, 208 mm; 55 slices.
Structural images were acquired using an MP2RAGE sequence with voxel size, 0.75 mm3; TR, 4300 ms; TE, 3.44 ms; 256 slices.

Imaging data were preprocessed using an adapted version of the MATLAB toolbox Data Processing Assistant for Resting-State fMRI (DPARSF V 3.0).
DICOM images were first converted to NIfTI format and realigned.
T1 images were reoriented, skull-stripped [FMRIB Software Library Brain Extraction Tool (FSL BET)], and coregistered to the NIfTI functional images using Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM8) functions.
Segmentation and the DARTEL algorithm were used to improve the estimation of non-neural signal in subject space and the spatial normalization.
From each gray matter voxel, the following signals were regressed: undesired linear trends, signals from the six head-motion parameters (three translation, three rotation), white matter, and CSF.
The CompCor method was used to regress out residual signal unrelated to neural activity (five principal components derived from noise regions-of-interest).
Global signal regression was not performed.
Single-subject functional images were subsequently normalized and smoothed using DARTEL (4 mm3).
Data processing steps also involved filtering (0.01–0.15 Hz) at a low-frequency component of the BOLD signal known to be sensitive to both resting-state and task-based functional connectivity.

Participants with head displacement ≥3 mm in ≥5% of volumes in any one scan were excluded.
Both resting-state and task-based data with frame-to-frame displacements of ≥0.40 mm were censored.
Participants with ≤85% of data remaining in any condition were excluded.

For each subject, regionally averaged time series were extracted for 264 spheres of 5 mm radius sampled across cortical and subcortical gray matter.
Spheres were positioned according to an existing brain parcellation and associated network definitions generated from a large cohort of participants (N ≈ 300).
For both sets of resting-state data (Pre-task and Post-task), functional connectivity was estimated using a temporal Pearson correlation between each pair of time series.
For the task-based functional connectivity analyses, a task regressor composed of the condition onsets modeled as boxcar functions convolved with a canonical hemodynamic response function was regressed from the time series.
After accounting for the hemodynamic lag, the residual time series from each 5 s reasoning period was concatenated to form in each brain region a condition-specific time series of interest.
A Pearson correlation was performed on the resulting regional time series for each condition separately, resulting in a 264 × 264 connectivity matrix for each subject.
Both resting-state and task-based matrices were converted to z scores.
Weighted graphs of proportional densities from the top 5% to the top 30% of connections were considered for analysis.

The degree of modularity in a network was characterized by the Q index, which represents the density of within-module connections relative to an appropriate random network null model.
Modules were identified using the Louvain greedy algorithm implemented in the Brain Connectivity Toolbox.

Global efficiency was computed as the inverse of the average characteristic path length between all nodes in a network and was used as an index of parallel information transfer.

A nonparametric Friedman test revealed a significant effect of reasoning complexity on both Latin Square Task accuracy and reaction time.
Bonferroni-corrected follow-up Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparisons were used.
A paired t test was performed between the Pre-task and Post-task resting-state data, and a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA was used to compare all four task states (Null, Binary, Ternary, Quaternary).
